sections.title: The doubt is already in the verb
sections.content: You know *dudo que* + subjunctive from B1 Unit 13 and *no creo que* from B1 Unit 7. Some verbs carry the doubt or the denial in their own meaning, so they need no *no*: *dudar que*, *negar que*, *desmentir que* and *poner en duda que* take the subjunctive. Put a *no* in front of them and the doubt is cancelled: you now accept the thing as true, so *no dudar que* and *no negar que* take the indicative. This is the mirror image of the opinion verbs in the last lesson.

sections.title: Doubt and denial, with and without no
rows: Dudo que venga. / Niego que lo sepa.
No dudo que viene. / No niego que lo sabe.
Doubt or denial cancelled: indicative. You accept it as true.
Creo que viene. / No creo que venga.
Compare: with an opinion verb it is the other way round. Affirmative: indicative. Negative: subjunctive.

sections.title: In the past
sections.content: As in B1 Unit 38, the subjunctive moves back when the main verb is in the past: *Negó que lo supiera*, *Dudaba que viniera*.

items.english: I doubt that Marta knows it.

items.spanish: No dudo que Marta lo sabe.
items.english: I do not doubt that Marta knows it.

items.spanish: El jefe negó que fuera su error.
items.english: The boss denied that it was his mistake.
Pablo denied that it was true.

items.spanish: Pongo en duda que sea una buena idea.
items.english: I question whether it is a good idea.

sections.content: With *no negar que* you will hear both moods. The indicative admits a fact (*No niego que es difícil*), and the subjunctive is also used, so learn the indicative first. With *no dudar que* the indicative is the rule.
